posts.note: Brain Stimulation 2025 Q&A recap for TMS clinicians. Mostly present-state science; forward-looking items are a Radial open house, a trial-timing call, coverage-policy claims, a registry announcement and a few hedged research-direction calls. Two present-state thesis claims logged with forward_looking false.
Panel recap (Leucter, Zangen, Hanlon) on midline TMS targets. One third-party trial expectation logged with own_claim false; one present-state thesis claim logged with forward_looking false.
Second midline-targets recap. Hedged calls about unmapped midline cortex plus a relayed INEMS workshop plan. One mechanistic claim logged with forward_looking false.
Personal essay on writing and loss. Only low-value personal or general claims; all three flagged borderline.

Definium DT120 (LSD) EMERGE MDD Phase 3 readout. Trial-timing calls for the Voyage GAD trial, capital-market thesis, direct calls that psychedelic medicines are coming with undeniable effect sizes, and a RAMHT event announcement.

Long-form buy-and-bill economics essay (draft version of a free post). Dense with calls about REMS guardrails, in-clinic distribution, monitoring, clinic infrastructure, reimbursement trends and who captures the economics; plus a dated FDA comment-period item.

statements.quote: Radial is having an Open House in Midtown Manhattan on Thursday, March 12th, 2026, at 10 w 37th St., so health professionals can learn about innovative treatments both available now (like SWIFT and SAINT TMS, PRISM, Proliv, Spravato), and those to come!
statements.context: Opening notice before the conference dispatch. The author announces an open house of Radial (his own company) for health professionals on 12 March 2026 in Midtown Manhattan, 4pm to 8pm EST, to present treatments available now and 'those to come'.
statements.note: Own-organization event announcement; coder likely marks CONTROL. 'those to come' implies future treatment offerings at Radial.

statements.quote: The difference between a protocol that requires staff from 7am to 6pm versus one that fits into a sensible 8-hour day is the difference between a protocol that’s academically interesting and one that will actually get delivered to patients at scale.
statements.context: Inter-session interval section. After Fitzgerald cites a human study on 15-minute intervals between iTBS sessions, the author argues that a shorter interval lets accelerated TMS fit an 8-hour clinic day, and that only such a protocol will be delivered to patients at scale.
statements.note: General claim about which accelerated TMS protocols reach scale; borderline.

statements.quote: Are We at the Ceiling? (For Regular TMS, Probably Yes. For TBS, Possibly No.)
statements.context: Section heading and thesis. The author argues the dose-response curve for standard 10 Hz rTMS is flat at the top (no gain from more pulses), while theta burst stimulation may still gain from dose optimization because pulse count has peaks and troughs.
statements.confidence_phrase: Probably Yes. For TBS, Possibly No.
statements.note: Borderline: dose-response assessment whose predictive reading is that TBS dosing can still improve outcomes while standard rTMS cannot.

statements.quote: Fitzgerald’s read: the **interval between sessions** is probably the most practically important variable we haven’t yet optimized. More important than pulse count per session. Possibly more important than targeting.
statements.context: Interval section conclusion. Fitzgerald's assessment, presented approvingly by the author, that optimizing the inter-session interval in accelerated TMS will matter more than pulse count or targeting.
statements.note: Attributed to Fitzgerald; the author endorses the interval's importance in the preceding paragraph. Coder may treat as third-party. Bold markers are in the source text.

statements.quote: There is now a named trial — the Kale Award trial — specifically designed to address whether bilateral stimulation is superior to unilateral for suicidal ideation. It’s years out from results.
statements.context: Right-sided stimulation and suicidality section. The author notes a named trial (Kale Award trial) that tests bilateral versus unilateral TMS for suicidal ideation and states its results are years away.
statements.note: Timing call on a trial readout.

statements.quote: Getting the angle right — maximizing the electric field penetration — may ultimately explain more outcome variance than the exact coordinates you’re targeting.
statements.context: Neuronavigation section. After Fitzgerald notes that DLPFC gyral orientation varies across people, the author (in his own voice, 'worth dwelling on') suggests coil angle and E-field optimization may ultimately explain more TMS outcome variance than target coordinates.
statements.note: Prediction about what future evidence will show; borderline scientific claim.

statements.quote: The more of those you file, the more you shift national coverage policy.
statements.context: Insurance section, the author's own speech from the conference floor about insurers that refuse to cover iTBS. He claims that filing independent medical review appeals plus state attorney general complaints shifts national insurer coverage policy for TMS.
statements.note: Conditional claim about advocacy effect on coverage policy; the author's own position ('I stand by it').

statements.quote: I have written about this extensively in this newsletter. I will keep writing about it.
statements.context: Insurance section. After stating that ERISA plan sponsors have had a fiduciary duty since 2021, the author commits to keep writing about it in The Frontier Psychiatrists.
statements.note: Own-newsletter commitment; low forecast value; coder likely marks CONTROL.

statements.quote: This is how coverage standards change. Not by accepting what the insurer says.
statements.context: Insurance section, end of the appeals path (appeal to independent medical review, write to the attorney general). The author asserts this process is how payer coverage standards for TMS and iTBS change.
statements.note: Restatement of the preceding claim that filing appeals and attorney general complaints shifts coverage policy.

statements.quote: There’s a registry being built, announced in this session. The goal is to aggregate non-invasive brain stimulation data from centers worldwide.
statements.context: Bigger Picture section. The author reports that a worldwide non-invasive brain stimulation registry is being built, announced at Brain Stimulation 2025, to answer questions that RCTs cannot.
statements.note: Relayed announcement of a future registry; the author endorses the need for it.

statements.quote: The optimal number of pulses is probably different for every person.
statements.context: 6,000-pulse section. The author highlights Fitzgerald's bolded claim, which he calls genuinely important, that the optimal TBS pulse count differs per patient.
statements.note: Present-state scientific hypothesis; no future state asserted. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: the standard left-DLPFC target, for all its merits, is probably not the right answer for everyone.
statements.context: Introduction. The author summarizes the shared conclusion of the Brain Stimulation 2025 panel (Leucter, Zangen, Hanlon) that the standard left DLPFC TMS target is probably not right for every patient; he adopts it in the closing section.
statements.note: Present-state clinical claim; no future state asserted. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: It might prove more effective and almost certainly would be more tolerable.
statements.context: The author's editorial note after Leucter's talk: right OFC targets are painful; the precuneus and posterior cingulate at the back of the head are lightly innervated. The author predicts a posterior midline (precuneus) target might prove more effective than OFC and would almost certainly be more tolerable.
statements.note: Compound: hedged efficacy call plus near-certain tolerability call for a target not yet in clinical use.

statements.quote: Early data suggest the strategies may converge on similar endpoints at the end of a full treatment course — but with an important caveat: the OFC approach seems to take longer to “kick in,” suggesting that if it’s going to be used, starting earlier in the course may matter.
statements.context: Leucter's ongoing open-label randomization at UCLA compares three augmentation strategies for early TMS non-responders (right OFC, right DLPFC, theta-burst priming of left DLPFC). Leucter's early read is that the strategies may end at similar endpoints.
statements.horizon_text: at the end of a full treatment course
statements.note: Third-party (Leucter) expectation about an ongoing trial, relayed by the author without explicit endorsement.

statements.quote: There is a clinical signal potentially sitting in this unmapped territory, and the field has largely walked past it.
statements.context: Close of the Hanlon talk summary on the midline strip: after 177 trials, large portions of the midline remain unstudied, and tolerability mapping shows most zones are well tolerated. The author's summary asserts a clinical signal potentially exists in the unstudied midline zones.
statements.note: Author's summary of Hanlon's closing; he restates it in his own voice in the 2026-03-10 post.

statements.quote: these are all pieces of a future precision psychiatry workflow that does not yet fully exist.
statements.context: 'A Pattern Worth Naming' section. The author lists Zangen's symptom clusters, evoked-response predictors, connectivity-based individualization and Leucter's measurement-based augmentation as pieces of a future precision psychiatry workflow for TMS target selection.
statements.note: Implies such a workflow will be built; borderline.

statements.quote: The midline, it turns out, is not just the space between the targets we already know. It’s where the next generation of the field is likely to be built.
statements.context: Closing line of the post. The author predicts the next generation of TMS and neuromodulation will be built on midline (medial and frontopolar) cortical targets.
statements.note: Author's own field-direction call.

statements.quote: The implication is that the frontopolar cortex isn’t just a reasonable target for addiction — it may be the mechanistic linchpin that ties together what have seemed like disparate TMS findings across substances and behavioral addictions.
statements.context: Addiction dual-target section. After a meta-analysis of over 2,000 trials linked effective addiction TMS protocols to frontopolar E-field engagement, the author draws the implication that the frontopolar cortex may be the mechanistic linchpin of TMS for addiction.
statements.note: Present-state mechanistic claim; no future state asserted. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: supporting the idea that connectivity mapping could one day guide not just target selection but coil orientation and dosing as well.
statements.context: Individualization section. In a sixty-participant fMRI study, frontopolar-to-reward connectivity predicted cue reactivity. The author says this supports the idea that connectivity mapping could one day guide target selection, coil orientation and dosing.
statements.note: Relays the presenter's idea in the author's own framing.

statements.quote: The midline story suggests there may be a significant clinical signal sitting right in front of us — or rather, right above the nasion.
statements.context: 'What Nobody Has Tried Yet' section. Large portions of the midline strip are unstudied after 177 trials and tolerability probing shows most zones are tolerable; the author suggests a significant clinical signal may sit in the unstimulated midline cortex.
statements.note: Restates the 2026-03-03 post's claim in the author's own voice.

statements.quote: announced a collaborative network (INEMS: the International Network on Non-invasive Electric and Magnetic Stimulation) with a planned workshop at the upcoming Brisbane meeting.
statements.context: 'A Global Effort' section. The presenter announced the INEMS network with a workshop planned for the upcoming Brisbane brain stimulation meeting; the author relays the plan.
statements.note: Relayed plan for a future event; not the author's own forecast.

statements.quote: For those of us in interventional psychiatry, the midline is no longer just the space between the targets we already know. It may be the next frontier!
statements.context: Closing line. The author's hedged call that midline cortical targets may be the next frontier of interventional psychiatry.
statements.note: Restatement of the 2026-03-03 closing call, hedged from 'likely' to 'may'.

statements.quote: Some tasks can’t be automated with AI. Artificial intelligence isn’t a time machine.
statements.context: Personal essay on interviews the author can no longer do with people who have died. He asserts AI cannot recover or reconstruct lived memories, so some writing tasks cannot be automated with AI.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense capability claim with a standing 'never' reading ('never know which ones you carried with you').

statements.quote: Writing about the real is a race against time I will surely lose, and only capture a whiff of the moment I had hoped to communicate.
statements.context: Personal essay. The author predicts he will lose the race to record real stories before his sources are gone.
statements.note: Personal; low forecast value.

statements.quote: I fret that I will change things by how I write about them. I hope, very much, that I will do the same for the things I’d like to see happen.
statements.context: Personal essay. The author voices a worry that his writing will change the things he writes about, and a hope that it will also change the things he wants to happen.
statements.note: Worry plus wish; hedged personal expectation; low forecast value.

statements.quote: Heck, we have a whole event series dedicated to them, with the next RAMHT event happening at Psych Congress, on September 14th, 2026. Get your tickets now!
statements.context: Aside about the author's Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatments (RAMHT) event series; the next event is announced for Psych Congress on 14 September 2026.
statements.note: Own-organization event announcement; coder likely marks CONTROL.

statements.quote: Much to the surprise of us all, their readout on their concurrent MDD clinical trial program happened before their GAD readout, which is expected later this year.
statements.context: Definium Therapeutics (CMO Dan Karlin) read out top-line Phase 3 data for DT120 (LSD, lysergide tartrate ODT) in MDD (EMERGE) the week before the post; the author says the GAD Phase 3 (Voyage) readout is expected later in 2026.
statements.note: Timing call on the Voyage GAD readout.

statements.quote: DT120 GAD pivotal (Voyage, NCT06741228): started December 11, 2024, primary completion projected July 2026. ~19 months.
statements.context: Bullet from the clinical trials registry as reported by the author: the DT120 generalized anxiety disorder pivotal trial Voyage is projected to reach primary completion in July 2026 (post dated 2 July 2026).
statements.note: Registry projection relayed and used as fact by the author; the underlying estimate is the registry's.

statements.quote: For investors, that means it’s possible to speed-run a clinical trial program, which means money is moving through the system faster. Returns on investment are quicker, and the time value of money goes up.
statements.context: 'Why the timeline matters' section. From Definium running its MDD pivotal in about 13 months, the author generalizes that psychedelic clinical trial programs can be speed-run and that investor returns come faster.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense generalization with a forward implication for capital flows.

statements.quote: The actual amount of time patients are likely to sit in an office is not outlandish.
statements.context: After noting that most EMERGE patients were no longer woozy after five or six hours rather than 12, the author expects that in-office time for DT120 (LSD) treatment in practice will not be outlandish.
statements.note: Hedged call about future clinic workflow for LSD-based treatment.

statements.quote: Speed of capital follows speed of evidence. If the next program in this company’s pipeline runs on the same clock, the implied cost of capital for psychedelic medicine drops—this is financially material. Every other CNS program may get benchmarked against it.
statements.context: 'Capital flows at trial speed' section, after Definium raised $805 million following the readout. Conditional call: if Definium's next program runs as fast, the cost of capital for psychedelic medicine drops and other CNS programs may be benchmarked against it.
statements.note: Compound conditional: cost-of-capital drop (if the condition holds) plus a hedged benchmarking claim.

statements.quote: Is it possible that this will work? I think the answer is yes. I think the psychedelic medicines are coming.
statements.context: Closing argument. After years of investor hand-wringing, the author states his belief that psychedelic medicines will reach patients and the market.
statements.note: Direct call; no date.

statements.quote: I think their effect sizes are going to be undeniable. They will be different in different patient populations, but we have at least 7 psychiatric disorder treatments—lysergide, comp360, ibogaine derivatives, methylone, DMT, 5-MEO-DMT, MDMA and it’s enantomers, all of which are looking as remarkable as GLP-1s are for metabolic disorders.
statements.context: Closing argument. The author predicts the effect sizes of psychedelic medicines (lysergide, COMP360, ibogaine derivatives, methylone, DMT, 5-MeO-DMT, MDMA and its enantiomers) will be undeniable and compares them to GLP-1s for metabolic disorders.
statements.note: Compound: efficacy call across seven psychedelic classes; GLP-1 comparison.

statements.quote: It is, however, great before we’ve even optimized workflows, business models, care pathways, patient experiences, adjunctive therapies, or any of the rest of the “must haves” when psychedelic research becomes psychedelic medicine.
statements.context: On Definium's EMERGE result: the author says the outcome is great before workflows, business models, care pathways, patient experiences and adjunctive therapies are optimized; this presupposes psychedelic research will become psychedelic medicine and that results can improve further.
statements.note: Presupposes a future transition to psychedelic medicine; implies later results improve with optimization.

statements.quote: Bigger, better results are possible for our patients.
statements.context: Closing lines after EMERGE. The author asserts that outcomes better than EMERGE's are possible once psychedelic medicine workflows mature.
statements.note: Hedged forward call; low specificity.

statements.quote: pharmaceutical companies and medical device companies are only gonna keep creating miracles if they make a hell of a lot of money in the process.
statements.context: Thesis setup. The author claims pharma and device companies will keep producing breakthrough psychiatric treatments only if they stay highly profitable.
statements.note: Conditional general claim.

statements.quote: J&J’s Spravato was the beginning of this process, at least in psychiatry, but it won’t be the end of it, and that, as you can tell, is what I’m arguing should happen.
statements.context: Buy-and-bill section. The author predicts Spravato (esketamine, Johnson & Johnson) will not be the last in-clinic, buy-and-bill psychiatric medication; more will follow with psychedelics.
statements.note: Mixed predictive and normative ('what I'm arguing should happen').

statements.quote: the financials of small pills versus the psychedelics and medical devices that are coming
statements.context: Supply-chain aside. The author presupposes that psychedelic drugs and medical devices are coming to psychiatry, and contrasts their economics with one-a-day pills.
statements.note: Presupposition embedded in a clause; restated more directly later in the post.

statements.quote: Every year, drug prices go up. Every year, physician reimbursement attempts to go down.
statements.context: Payment section. The author states standing trends: drug prices rise every year and physician (Medicare) reimbursement trends flat or down, so buy-and-bill margins per unit of physician time shrink.
statements.note: Habitual trend claim; the predictive reading is continuation of the trend. Borderline.

statements.quote: The above compounds might have repeated dosing, but on the order of 1 to 4 doses in a year, not twice a week for the first month and more thereafter.
statements.context: Lifetime-value section. The author expects pipeline psychedelics (MDMA, LSD, psilocybin, ibogaine, methylone) to be dosed about 1 to 4 times a year, unlike Spravato's frequent dosing, which lowers patient lifetime value for clinics.
statements.note: Hedged dosing-frequency call.

statements.quote: hope the S code reimbursement keeps up, and then get paid a decreasing amount every year to observe a patient getting this treatment.
statements.context: 'The squeeze' summary. Under commercial plans with an S code for Spravato, the author expects clinics to pay more for the drug each year while observation reimbursement decreases every year.
statements.note: Restatement of the yearly drug-price-up, reimbursement-down trend.

statements.quote: The entire premise of this essay is that psychiatrists are likely to respond to incentives in the same way as every other human, and act accordingly. They will prescribe more of what I suspect will be better treatments.
statements.context: Incentive section, after the oncology buy-and-bill comparison. The author predicts that, given margin-on-drug incentives, psychiatrists will prescribe more psychedelic treatments, which he suspects will be better treatments.
statements.note: Compound: behavioral prediction conditional on incentives, plus a hedged efficacy claim.

statements.quote: It’s because psychedelics are all going to come with guardrails. These are in the form of Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (”REMS”).
statements.context: The author predicts all psychedelic medicines will come with REMS guardrails on dispensing and monitoring, as Spravato does, which will limit margin-on-drug abuse.
statements.note: Direct regulatory call.

statements.quote: Novel psychedelics coming to the world of clinical care, if the universe has been listening to me rant, will come with monitoring built in, likely with even more auditable video.
statements.context: REMS section. The author predicts novel psychedelics entering clinical care will carry built-in monitoring requirements, likely including auditable video.
statements.note: Hedged by the aside 'if the universe has been listening to me rant'.

statements.quote: Not only will pharmaceutical companies bring these drugs to market with the ability to have a sense of what’s happening in the room, but so will the third-party payors with whom we partner (with occasional consternation) to bring care to our patients.
statements.context: REMS section. The author predicts both pharma companies and third-party payers will have visibility (monitoring) into the treatment room during psychedelic dosing sessions.
statements.note: Extends the monitoring prediction to payers.

statements.quote: Almost all of them will require longer monitoring than we can currently account for.
statements.context: On the pipeline drugs behind Spravato (psilocybin, LSD, MDMA based): the author predicts almost all will require monitoring longer than current billing codes cover (two-hour 99417 MUE limit, six-hour CPT III limit).
statements.note: Follows the 'pipeline drugs that are coming behind Spravato' setup.

statements.quote: None of these drugs are gonna go through a retail pharmacy.
statements.context: Pipeline psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD, MDMA based) will not be dispensed through retail pharmacies; the author says they are in-clinic by design.
statements.note: Negative call; restated next as 'These treatments are in-clinic by design.'

statements.quote: These treatments are in-clinic by design. The clinic is the distribution channel.
statements.context: Immediately after the CVS and psilocybin joke; the author asserts psychedelic treatments will be delivered in clinics, which makes clinics the distribution channel for the drugs.
statements.note: Restatement of the preceding retail-pharmacy call; present tense about a future class of drugs.

statements.quote: These clinics are going to need extra rooms, and even more extra rooms, because if they don’t have enough extra rooms, we’re not gonna be able to help all the people who need it. Those rooms may need special cameras, IT infrastructure, comfortable furniture for an entire day of treatment.
statements.context: The author predicts psychedelic clinics will need many additional treatment rooms with cameras, IT infrastructure and day-long furniture; otherwise demand will not be met.
statements.confidence_phrase: are going to need ... may need
statements.note: Compound infrastructure call.

statements.quote: Somebody has to pay for all of that, and whoever pays for the rooms owns the economics of the distribution channel.
statements.context: The author claims whoever funds psychedelic clinic infrastructure (physicians, payer conglomerates such as Optum, or nobody) will own the distribution economics of psychedelic medicine.
statements.note: Followed by three candidate scenarios: physicians, conglomerates acquiring physicians, or only the wealthy get access.

statements.quote: if we don’t become a viable part of the actual business of business, our patients don’t get to have any good new stuff.
statements.context: Buy-and-bill section. Conditional prediction: unless psychiatrists take part in the business side, patients will not get new treatments.
statements.note: Conditional; borderline rhetorical.

statements.quote: We can stay terrible at it, and Optum and its colleagues will be happy to handle all the details and pocket all the dollars. Or we can get good at business while we still have the leverage.
statements.context: Closing argument. If physicians stay bad at business, Optum (UnitedHealth Group) and similar conglomerates will capture the economics of psychedelic care; the author implies physician leverage is time-limited ('while we still have the leverage').
statements.note: Conditional scenario; implies physician leverage will fade.

statements.quote: I’m willing to bet they’d prefer the set and setting of a clinic owned and operated by physicians over the set and setting you’d expect from the companies that brought you prior authorization of Zoloft.
statements.context: Closing. The author bets patients would prefer physician-owned psychedelic clinics over ones owned by payer conglomerates.
statements.note: Preference claim framed as a bet; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: The FDA is considering how psychedelics get regulated before any of them, officially, have been, and there’s an open comment period coming up on September 14th.
statements.context: P.S. The author states the FDA is considering psychedelic regulation before any psychedelic has been approved, and that an FDA open comment period is coming up on 14 September (2026); he asks readers to comment.
statements.note: Dated regulatory-process call; also states no psychedelic is officially regulated or approved as of the post.
